stem: You are the intern on an evening cover shift at a metropolitan general hospital with a busy medical ward and a registrar on site overnight. A nurse calls about a 32-year-old man with type 1 diabetes admitted this afternoon with gastroenteritis. He is on insulin glargine 22 units at night and insulin aspart with meals. He has vomited twice since arrival and has eaten almost nothing. His blood glucose is 9.8 mmol/L and capillary ketones are 0.4 mmol/L. Observations are normal and he is tolerating sips of water. The nurse asks whether she should give tonight's glargine, which is due in 30 minutes.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate instruction for his insulin tonight?

options.text: Withhold all insulin until he is eating and drinking normally and his vomiting has settled
Give the usual glargine dose, withhold mealtime aspart and monitor glucose and ketones
Withhold glargine and manage with supplemental aspart according to 4-hourly glucose readings
Give half the usual mealtime aspart dose now and withhold glargine until the morning

explanations.A: Withholding all insulin in a person with type 1 diabetes removes basal insulin and leads to ketosis and diabetic ketoacidosis within hours, regardless of oral intake.
explanations.B: Basal insulin must continue in type 1 diabetes even when the patient is not eating, because it suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis; mealtime insulin is withheld while intake is poor, and close glucose and ketone monitoring detects early deterioration.
explanations.C: Supplemental rapid-acting insulin alone cannot replace basal insulin; reactive sliding-scale insulin without a basal dose is associated with hyperglycaemia, ketosis and hypoglycaemia swings.
explanations.D: Mealtime aspart without a meal risks hypoglycaemia, and omitting glargine still leaves him without basal cover overnight.

learning_point: In type 1 diabetes, basal insulin is never withheld because the patient is not eating; withhold or reduce only the mealtime doses and monitor glucose and ketones closely.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetes
references.locator: Type 1 diabetes: managing insulin during intercurrent illness

references.title: Australian Diabetes Society: Peri-operative diabetes management guidelines
references.locator: Basal insulin continuation

tutor_context: Key fact: people with type 1 diabetes are absolutely insulin deficient and need basal insulin at all times. Common misconception: insulin is 'for food' and can be skipped when not eating. Ketones 0.4 mmol/L is normal; rising ketones above 0.6 mmol/L or glucose above 15 mmol/L with symptoms should prompt escalation to the registrar. Out of scope: DKA protocol details and insulin dose titration.
plan: Tests the single fact that basal insulin continues in type 1 diabetes during poor oral intake, evidencing 4.1 and 1.8. Setting is an evening cover call from a ward nurse with a registrar available. Distractors are withholding all insulin, sliding scale alone, and giving prandial insulin without food. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Diabetes and the ADS peri-operative guideline.

stem: You are the intern on the general ward of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula. The 4-bed emergency department is staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. A 29-year-old woman was admitted for observation after collapsing without warning while sitting at a family barbecue. She recovered within a minute, has no injuries and no past medical history. Her examination is normal and her lying and standing blood pressures are unchanged. She asks whether she can go home. Her 12-lead ECG, taken in the department, is in her notes. You know that some ECG findings in syncope mandate discussion with the GP on call and consideration of transfer for cardiology assessment rather than discharge.
lead_in: Which ECG finding is a high-risk feature that requires escalation before she is discharged?

options.text: Sinus bradycardia at 56 beats per minute
Incomplete right bundle branch block pattern in lead V1
Corrected QT interval of 520 milliseconds
Sinus arrhythmia with respiration

explanations.A: Sinus bradycardia in the mid-50s is common in a healthy young adult and, without pauses or heart block, is not a high-risk feature.
explanations.B: Incomplete right bundle branch block is a normal variant in young people and does not by itself indicate an arrhythmic cause of syncope.
explanations.C: A corrected QT interval above 500 milliseconds indicates long QT and a risk of torsades de pointes; syncope while seated with a prolonged QTc is a red flag for arrhythmic syncope and requires monitoring and specialist discussion.
explanations.D: Sinus arrhythmia is a normal physiological finding and not a marker of cardiac syncope.

learning_point: Syncope without warning while seated plus any ECG abnormality such as QTc above 500 ms, pre-excitation, Brugada pattern, high-grade block or ventricular pre-excitation is high risk and must be escalated rather than discharged.
setting_note: In a rural hospital with no cardiology or telemetry on site, a high-risk ECG means continuous monitoring in the department, discussion with the GP on call and a cardiology or MedSTAR call about transfer to Adelaide; a tertiary hospital can admit to a monitored bed and obtain echocardiography the same day.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Syncope: assessment and risk stratification

references.title: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: position statement on the management of syncope
references.locator: High-risk ECG features

tutor_context: Key facts: red-flag features are syncope during exertion or while supine or seated, no prodrome, palpitations before the event, family history of sudden death, structural heart disease, and an abnormal ECG (QTc over 500 ms or under 340 ms, Brugada pattern, WPW, bifascicular block, Mobitz II or complete heart block, sustained bradycardia under 40). Misconception: a young patient with a normal examination can always go home. Out of scope: management of long QT syndrome.
plan: Tests recall of high-risk ECG criteria in syncope (4.1, 1.5). Scene is a rural ward where discharge decisions fall to the intern with a GP on call. Distractors are normal variants a junior doctor might misread as pathological. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular and the CSANZ syncope statement.

stem: You are the intern on an evening cover shift at a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward, on-site CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. The physician is available by phone. A 34-year-old woman presents to the ward clerk's desk asking to be seen because she was discharged from this hospital 5 weeks ago with newly diagnosed Graves disease and started on carbimazole 30 mg daily. Over 2 days she has developed a sore throat, mouth ulcers and fevers to 38.6 °C. Heart rate is 104, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 98%. Her throat is red without exudate and she has no neck stiffness or rash. She took her carbimazole this morning.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin for pharyngitis, continue carbimazole and arrange GP review in 2 days
Replace carbimazole with propylthiouracil and send a thyroid function test
Reassure her that viral pharyngitis is likely, continue carbimazole and advise paracetamol and fluids
Withhold carbimazole, send an urgent full blood count and discuss with the physician on call

explanations.A: Oral antibiotics and continued carbimazole in a febrile patient on an antithyroid drug ignores the possibility of agranulocytosis; if neutropenic she needs the drug stopped and intravenous antibiotics, not GP review in 2 days.
explanations.B: Propylthiouracil carries the same risk of agranulocytosis and cross-reactivity, so swapping drugs without checking the neutrophil count exposes her to the same danger.
explanations.C: Reassurance without a neutrophil count is unsafe; fever, sore throat and mouth ulcers in the first 3 months of carbimazole are the classic presentation of agranulocytosis.
explanations.D: Carbimazole-induced agranulocytosis typically presents with fever and sore throat in the first weeks of treatment; the drug must be withheld immediately, an urgent neutrophil count obtained and the physician involved so that intravenous antibiotics for neutropenic sepsis and transfer can be arranged if the count is low.

learning_point: Fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers in a patient recently started on carbimazole or propylthiouracil means withhold the drug and obtain an urgent neutrophil count the same day.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the full blood count may need to be run urgently on the on-site analyser or sent with a priority courier; if she is neutropenic she needs intravenous antibiotics within an hour and discussion with the physician and MedSTAR about transfer, because there is no ICU on site.

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Carbimazole: adverse effects and patient counselling (agranulocytosis)

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology
references.locator: Hyperthyroidism: antithyroid drug adverse effects

tutor_context: Key facts: agranulocytosis affects about 0.2 to 0.5% of patients on antithyroid drugs, usually within 3 months; patients should be counselled at the start to stop the drug and seek urgent review if fever or sore throat develops. Neutrophils below 0.5 x 10^9/L with fever is neutropenic sepsis and is treated as per the sepsis pathway. Misconception: a sore throat is just a viral illness. Out of scope: definitive management of Graves disease.
plan: Tests the decision to withhold an antithyroid drug and check the neutrophil count in a febrile patient (4.1, 1.8, 1.9). The rural evening setting makes early escalation matter because neutropenic sepsis would need transfer. Distractors are treating as pharyngitis, swapping to propylthiouracil and reassurance. Supported by AMH carbimazole monograph and Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 38-year-old Aboriginal man presents with 3 months of weight loss despite a good appetite, palpitations, heat intolerance and tremor. He has travelled from a regional community to visit family and has been offered support from the Aboriginal Liaison Officer, which he accepts. Heart rate is 112 and regular, blood pressure 138/70, temperature 37.1 °C. He has a fine tremor, warm moist palms and a smooth diffusely enlarged thyroid without nodules. His thyroid function results return: TSH less than 0.01 mIU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0), free T4 48 pmol/L (reference 10 to 20), free T3 18 pmol/L (reference 3.5 to 6.5).
lead_in: Which diagnosis do these thyroid function results indicate?

options.text: Primary hyperthyroidism
Primary hypothyroidism
Subclinical hyperthyroidism
Secondary (central) hyperthyroidism

explanations.A: A suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and free T3 shows the thyroid is overproducing hormone independently of pituitary drive, which is primary (overt) hyperthyroidism; with a diffuse goitre and no nodules, Graves disease is the likely cause.
explanations.B: Primary hypothyroidism produces a raised TSH with a low free T4, the opposite pattern to these results.
explanations.C: Subclinical hyperthyroidism is defined by a suppressed TSH with free T4 and free T3 within the reference range; here both are clearly elevated.
explanations.D: Central hyperthyroidism from a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma gives a raised or inappropriately normal TSH with high free T4; a suppressed TSH excludes it.

learning_point: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and free T3 is overt primary hyperthyroidism; TSH moves in the opposite direction to peripheral hormone in primary thyroid disease.
secondary_areas: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

references.title: RCPA Manual: Thyroid function tests
references.locator: Interpretation of TSH, free T4 and free T3 patterns

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology
references.locator: Hyperthyroidism: diagnosis

tutor_context: Key fact: in primary thyroid disease TSH and free T4 move in opposite directions; TSH is the most sensitive first-line test. Misconception: confusing the direction of TSH change. Culturally safe care includes offering the Aboriginal Liaison Officer and planning follow-up that works for a patient returning to a regional community. Out of scope: TSH receptor antibodies, uptake scans and choice of antithyroid therapy.
plan: Tests interpretation of a classic thyroid function pattern (4.1, 1.5), with culturally safe engagement shown as routine care (1.3). Tertiary ED setting. Distractors are the other three TFT patterns an intern may confuse. Supported by the RCPA Manual and Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident covering the wards overnight at a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula with a 4-bed emergency department staffed overnight by one junior doctor, with the GP on call at home 15 minutes away. At 0200 a nurse calls you to a 68-year-old man admitted 2 days ago with a community-acquired pneumonia. He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation and has just passed a large black tarry stool and feels light-headed. Heart rate is 112, blood pressure 94/58, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C. He is pale with a soft abdomen and no peritonism. He has one 22-gauge cannula in situ. The nearest endoscopy service is in Adelaide.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start an oral proton pump inhibitor, keep him nil by mouth and continue 4-hourly observations until the morning round
Insert a nasogastric tube and perform gastric lavage to confirm the bleeding source
Insert two large-bore cannulas, send a crossmatch, start crystalloid, withhold apixaban and call the GP on call and MedSTAR
Give intravenous tranexamic acid, keep him nil by mouth and book endoscopy on the next visiting specialist list

explanations.A: He is haemodynamically unstable with melaena on an anticoagulant; oral acid suppression and 4-hourly observations do not address shock or the need for endoscopy and transfer.
explanations.B: Nasogastric lavage is not recommended for diagnosis in upper gastrointestinal bleeding and delays resuscitation and escalation.
explanations.C: Shock from an anticoagulant-associated upper gastrointestinal bleed needs immediate intravenous access, crossmatch, fluid resuscitation, withholding the anticoagulant and early escalation; in a hospital without endoscopy or blood bank depth this means calling the GP on call and the retrieval service without delay.
explanations.D: Tranexamic acid has not been shown to benefit gastrointestinal bleeding and increases thromboembolic risk, and waiting for a visiting list ignores the urgency of an unstable bleed.

learning_point: An unstable upper gastrointestinal bleed is resuscitated with two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch and fluids while anticoagulation is withheld and senior help and retrieval are called at once.
setting_note: In a rural hospital without endoscopy the resident's priorities are resuscitation, early use of any on-site emergency O-negative blood if needed, and an early MedSTAR call because transfer to Adelaide takes hours; in a tertiary hospital the gastroenterology registrar is called and urgent endoscopy can occur on site.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal
references.locator: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding: initial resuscitation and management of anticoagulated patients

references.title: SA Health Rapid Detection and Response observation chart and escalation criteria
references.locator: Systolic blood pressure and heart rate triggers for medical review

tutor_context: Key facts: melaena plus tachycardia and hypotension is a major bleed; apixaban is withheld and reversal (andexanet or prothrombin complex concentrate) is discussed with haematology for life-threatening bleeding; intravenous PPI is reasonable after resuscitation but is not the first priority. Misconception: oral PPI and watchful waiting is adequate overnight. Out of scope: endoscopic haemostasis techniques.
plan: Tests the immediate resuscitation and escalation sequence for an unstable anticoagulated upper gastrointestinal bleed (4.1, 1.9). The scene is a single-doctor rural hospital where retrieval must be called early. Distractors are passive observation, obsolete nasogastric lavage and tranexamic acid with delayed endoscopy. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal and SA Health RDR criteria.

stem: You are the intern in the pre-admission clinic of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, which has a 4-bed emergency department staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. You are clerking a 38-year-old woman booked for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the visiting surgeon's list in 10 days. She mentions that 11 weeks ago she had a proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg after a long flight and has been taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily since. Her haemoglobin and renal function are normal and she has no bleeding history. The surgeon and anaesthetist are in Adelaide and the list is finalised by the end of today. You also need to complete her medication chart, consent paperwork and group and hold.
lead_in: Which action should you prioritise before she leaves the clinic?

options.text: Instruct her to stop apixaban 48 hours before surgery as per the hospital's standard anticoagulant interruption guide
Phone the surgeon and anaesthetist today about the recent deep vein thrombosis and apixaban so they can decide on timing
Request a repeat lower limb Doppler ultrasound to confirm the thrombus has resolved before she is listed for theatre
Request a thrombophilia screen so the result is available for the anaesthetist at her review next week

explanations.A: Interrupting anticoagulation within 3 months of a proximal deep vein thrombosis carries a high risk of recurrence or embolism, and the decision about whether to defer elective surgery or bridge is a senior one; an intern should not apply the standard interruption guide unaided.
explanations.B: A venous thromboembolism within the past 3 months is a recognised reason to consider deferring elective surgery or arranging specialist advice on perioperative anticoagulation; because the list is finalised today and the team is off site, escalating now gives the surgeon and anaesthetist the chance to change the plan before she is committed to theatre.
explanations.C: Repeat imaging does not change the decision about interrupting anticoagulation and delays the conversation that matters.
explanations.D: Thrombophilia testing on anticoagulation is unreliable and does not alter perioperative management; it is not an intern-level decision to order in this context.

learning_point: Recent venous thromboembolism on anticoagulation is a perioperative red flag that must be escalated to the surgical and anaesthetic team before the elective list is finalised, not managed by applying a standard interruption protocol.
setting_note: In a rural hospital the surgeon and anaesthetist visit from Adelaide, so the intern often has only one opportunity to raise concerns by phone before the list is locked; in a tertiary hospital the anaesthetic pre-admission clinic and a haematology service are on site and can review the patient directly.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Perioperative management of anticoagulant therapy: direct oral anticoagulants and recent venous thromboembolism

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Apixaban: practice points on surgery and interruption

tutor_context: Key facts: the risk of recurrent thrombosis is highest in the first 3 months after an acute venous thromboembolism; elective surgery is usually deferred beyond this period, and if it cannot be deferred, specialist advice on interruption and bridging is needed. Misconception: direct oral anticoagulants can always be stopped 48 hours before surgery. Out of scope: specific bridging regimens and inferior vena cava filters.
plan: Tests prioritising escalation of a perioperative anticoagulation problem over routine clerking tasks (4.1, 1.7, 2.4). The rural pre-admission clinic with an off-site surgical team makes timely escalation the decisive act. Distractors are protocol-driven interruption, unnecessary imaging and an inappropriate thrombophilia screen. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular and AMH.

stem: You are the intern on the surgical ward of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. On the morning round the registrar asks you to review the medication chart of a 30-year-old man, weight 88 kg, who is day 1 after a laparoscopic appendicectomy for perforated appendicitis. He is on intravenous antibiotics and is expected to stay at least 3 more days. He is mobilising only to the bathroom because of pain. He has no history of bleeding, his platelet count is 260 x 10^9/L and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m2. The registrar notes that no venous thromboembolism prophylaxis has been charted and asks you to fix this before you move on.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate prescription to add to his chart?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally once daily
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily
Graduated compression stockings alone with early mobilisation
Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily

explanations.A: Aspirin is not recommended as sole venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for general surgical inpatients; it is inferior to low molecular weight heparin.
explanations.B: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily is a treatment dose for established thrombosis and would expose a postoperative patient to unnecessary bleeding risk.
explanations.C: Mechanical prophylaxis alone is reserved for patients with a contraindication to anticoagulants; he has no bleeding risk and has multiple thrombosis risk factors.
explanations.D: A postoperative patient with intra-abdominal infection and reduced mobility is at moderate to high risk of venous thromboembolism; standard prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg once daily with normal renal function is the recommended pharmacological prophylaxis, combined with encouraging mobilisation.

learning_point: Surgical inpatients at increased venous thromboembolism risk without bleeding contraindications should be charted prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily (dose adjusted for renal impairment or extremes of weight).

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in surgical patients

references.title: Venous Thromboembolism Prevention Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Quality statements on risk assessment and prevention

tutor_context: Key facts: every inpatient should have documented VTE risk assessment; enoxaparin 40 mg daily is standard prophylaxis, reduced to 20 mg daily when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min; mechanical prophylaxis is added or used alone when bleeding risk is high. Misconception: young patients do not need prophylaxis. Out of scope: extended prophylaxis after cancer surgery and orthopaedic regimens.
plan: Tests safe charting of standard pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (4.1, 1.8) in a tertiary surgical ward. Distractors are aspirin, a treatment dose and mechanical prophylaxis alone. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular and the ACSQHC VTE Prevention Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident on the medical ward of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, which has a 4-bed emergency department staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. A 79-year-old man with Parkinson disease was admitted 3 days ago after a witnessed aspiration during a meal, with right lower lobe consolidation on chest X-ray. The locum overnight started intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 8-hourly. He is now afebrile for 36 hours, eating a modified diet with speech pathology input, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and C-reactive protein has fallen from 180 to 70 mg/L. Blood cultures at 48 hours are negative. He has normal renal function and no antibiotic allergies. The GP on call asks you to rationalise his antibiotics on today's round.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Change to oral amoxicillin to complete 5 days in total and document the stop date
Continue intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam to complete 7 days because he is responding well to it
Change to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate plus metronidazole for 10 days to cover anaerobes
Continue intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for 5 days then step down to oral ciprofloxacin

explanations.A: Aspiration pneumonia in a patient without hospital-acquired risk factors is treated the same as community-acquired pneumonia; once he is improving, afebrile and swallowing, intravenous therapy should be stepped down to oral amoxicillin and total duration kept to 5 days, with the stop date written on the chart.
explanations.B: Clinical response is not a reason to continue a broad-spectrum antipseudomonal agent; this is unnecessary spectrum, unnecessary intravenous access and more days than needed.
explanations.C: Routine anaerobic cover is not recommended for aspiration pneumonia unless there is lung abscess, empyema or severe periodontal disease, and 10 days is longer than guidelines advise.
explanations.D: Fluoroquinolones have no role in step-down for uncomplicated pneumonia; they carry significant adverse effects and resistance pressure, and 5 days of intravenous therapy is excessive when he can swallow.

learning_point: Rationalising antibiotics means narrowing the spectrum, switching to oral when the patient is improving and can swallow, setting a short total duration, and documenting the stop date.
setting_note: In a rural hospital without an on-site infectious diseases service the resident can seek advice from the antimicrobial stewardship pharmacist or the physician by phone, but the step-down decision is within a PGY2's scope using Therapeutic Guidelines; in a tertiary hospital the stewardship team may review broad-spectrum prescriptions daily.

generation.uncertainty_note: Therapeutic Guidelines treats aspiration pneumonia as community-acquired pneumonia without routine anaerobic cover; some local guidelines still favour amoxicillin-clavulanate, which would also be acceptable oral step-down but does not change the key principle of narrowing and shortening therapy.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Aspiration pneumonia and community-acquired pneumonia: intravenous to oral switch and duration

references.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Quality statements on review of therapy, intravenous to oral switch and documentation

tutor_context: Key facts: criteria for intravenous to oral switch are clinical improvement, afebrile, able to swallow and absorb, and no deep-seated infection; total duration for uncomplicated pneumonia is 5 days (or 3 days after clinical stability). Anaerobic cover is reserved for abscess or empyema. Misconception: broad-spectrum therapy that is working should be completed unchanged. Out of scope: hospital-acquired pneumonia regimens and penicillin allergy pathways.
plan: Tests a nuanced stewardship decision: de-escalate an inappropriately broad regimen for aspiration pneumonia (1.8, 1.7). The rural ward with a GP on call makes the resident the person making and documenting the decision. Distractors each preserve a common error: completing broad-spectrum therapy, adding anaerobic cover, or step-down to a fluoroquinolone. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the ACSQHC AMS Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident on the surgical ward of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, which has a 4-bed emergency department staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. A 36-year-old man is day 3 after an open repair of an incarcerated inguinal hernia and is recovering well on oral analgesia. On the night of surgery he had a single temperature of 38.1 °C and the covering doctor took one set of blood cultures from a freshly inserted cannula. Today he is afebrile, heart rate 72, blood pressure 124/78, wound clean, eating and mobilising. The laboratory phones to report that the aerobic bottle of the single set has grown coagulase-negative staphylococci at 52 hours; the anaerobic bottle is negative. He is on no antibiotics.
lead_in: What does this blood culture result most likely represent?

options.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia requiring intravenous vancomycin
Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia requiring at least 14 days of intravenous antibiotics
Skin contamination at the time of collection, with no antibiotic treatment indicated
Polymicrobial surgical sepsis requiring broadening to piperacillin-tazobactam

explanations.A: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are a different organism from Staphylococcus aureus; methicillin resistance in a skin commensal does not make it a pathogen in this context.
explanations.B: A true Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia is coagulase positive and would be treated seriously, but this organism is coagulase negative and the patient is well.
explanations.C: Coagulase-negative staphylococci growing in one bottle of a single set after more than 48 hours in a well patient without a prosthetic device or central line is the typical pattern of skin contamination during collection; no antibiotics are needed, and the finding should be documented with the reasoning.
explanations.D: A single skin commensal is not polymicrobial growth, and the patient has no clinical features of sepsis to justify broad-spectrum therapy.

learning_point: Coagulase-negative staphylococci in one bottle of one set after a long time to positivity in a well patient without intravascular devices is almost always a contaminant and does not warrant antibiotics.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Principles of antimicrobial use: interpreting culture results and contaminants

references.title: RCPA Manual: Blood culture
references.locator: Interpretation, contamination and time to positivity

tutor_context: Key facts: features favouring contamination are growth in one of multiple bottles or sets, time to positivity beyond 48 hours, a skin commensal and a well patient without prosthetic material or a central venous catheter. Always take two sets from separate sites to help interpretation. Misconception: every positive blood culture needs antibiotics. Out of scope: management of coagulase-negative staphylococcal infection of prosthetic devices.
plan: Tests interpretation of a likely contaminant blood culture (1.5, 1.8). Rural surgical ward setting where the resident must decide without calling the laboratory registrar. Distractors conflate the organism with Staphylococcus aureus, MRSA or polymicrobial sepsis. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the RCPA Manual.

stem: You are the sole junior doctor overnight at a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula with a 4-bed emergency department; the GP on call is at home 20 minutes away. At 0100 a 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 12 hours of rapidly spreading redness of the right calf and severe pain that seems out of proportion to the appearance. Heart rate is 118, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 24, temperature 38.9 °C, oxygen saturation 95%. The skin over the calf is tense and dusky with two haemorrhagic bullae, and the tenderness extends beyond the erythema. Venous lactate is 3.6 mmol/L. At the same time a teenager with a deformed wrist is waiting to be seen and a ward nurse asks you to chart a sedative for a restless patient.
lead_in: What should you do first?

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly for cellulitis, admit him to the ward and hand over to the GP in the morning
Request a plain X-ray of the leg to look for soft tissue gas before deciding whether to escalate to the GP on call
Mark the edge of the erythema, elevate the leg, start intravenous fluids and antibiotics and reassess the limb in 2 hours
Start intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics now, and call both the GP on call and MedSTAR for retrieval

explanations.A: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, haemorrhagic bullae, tenderness beyond the erythema and septic shock point to necrotising fasciitis, not simple cellulitis; flucloxacillin alone and morning review would be fatal delay.
explanations.B: Imaging is insensitive for necrotising fasciitis and must not delay antibiotics, resuscitation or the surgical referral that is the definitive treatment.
explanations.C: Marking and reassessing is appropriate for uncomplicated cellulitis but a patient with hypotension, raised lactate and necrotising features needs escalation now, not in 2 hours.
explanations.D: Suspected necrotising fasciitis with septic shock is a time-critical surgical emergency; the single doctor must start resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin as per Therapeutic Guidelines) and simultaneously call for senior help and retrieval, because debridement cannot happen in this hospital. The wrist and the sedative chart wait or are delegated.

learning_point: Pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading dusky skin, bullae and shock mean necrotising fasciitis; start broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluids and call for surgical transfer immediately, ahead of every less urgent task.
setting_note: In a rural hospital with no surgeon on site the earliest MedSTAR call determines time to debridement, which drives survival; a tertiary emergency department would activate the sepsis pathway and call the surgical and intensive care registrars to the bedside.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Necrotising skin and soft tissue infections: empirical therapy and urgent surgical referral

references.title: SA Health Rapid Detection and Response escalation criteria
references.locator: Hypotension and tachycardia triggers for immediate medical emergency response

references.title: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Time-critical management and escalation

tutor_context: Key facts: necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis; red flags are pain disproportionate to findings, rapid progression, bullae, crepitus, skin anaesthesia, systemic toxicity and raised lactate. Empirical therapy is meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (clindamycin for toxin suppression). Definitive treatment is surgical debridement. Misconception: imaging is needed to confirm before escalating. Out of scope: surgical technique and ICU management.
plan: Tests prioritisation under competing demands: recognising necrotising fasciitis with shock as the task that trumps everything else and escalating immediately (1.9, 1.8, 2.8). The single-doctor rural ED makes the retrieval call the key act. Distractors treat as cellulitis, defer to imaging or reassess later. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic, SA Health RDR criteria and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with a visiting surgeon and physician and specialist advice by phone. A 27-year-old woman presents with 4 days of fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed today by a blotchy red maculopapular rash that began on her face and is spreading down her trunk. She returned from a holiday in South-East Asia 10 days ago and says she never received childhood vaccinations. On examination she has small white spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars. She is sitting in the open waiting area and the triage nurse asks what precautions are needed while you arrange her assessment.
lead_in: Which transmission-based precautions are required for this patient?

options.text: Standard precautions with hand hygiene and a surgical mask for the patient while she waits in the open area
Airborne precautions in a closed single room, with fit-checked P2/N95 respirators and immune staff only
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask for staff within 1 metre of her and a surgical mask for the patient
Contact precautions with a gown and gloves for staff, dedicated patient equipment and a single room

explanations.A: Standard precautions alone do not protect against an airborne virus that can remain suspended in a room for up to 2 hours after the patient leaves.
explanations.B: Fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a cephalocaudal rash in an unvaccinated returned traveller is measles until proven otherwise; measles is transmitted by the airborne route, so she needs airborne precautions (negative pressure room where available, otherwise a single room with the door closed), P2/N95 respirators and exclusion of non-immune staff, together with urgent notification to the Communicable Disease Control Branch.
explanations.C: Droplet precautions are used for influenza and meningococcal disease; they are insufficient for measles because the virus travels on small airborne particles over longer distances.
explanations.D: Contact precautions are for organisms spread by touch such as multi-resistant organisms and Clostridioides difficile, not for airborne respiratory viruses.

learning_point: Suspected measles requires airborne precautions (single room, door closed, P2/N95 respirator, immune staff only) and immediate telephone notification to public health on clinical suspicion.
setting_note: A regional emergency department may have no negative pressure room, so the patient is placed in a single room with the door closed and the room is left vacant for 2 hours after she leaves; in a tertiary hospital a negative pressure isolation room is used.

references.title: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (NHMRC/ACSQHC)
references.locator: Transmission-based precautions: airborne precautions

references.title: SA Health: Measles - notification and public health management
references.locator: Notifiable on clinical suspicion by telephone to the Communicable Disease Control Branch; isolation requirements

references.title: Australian Immunisation Handbook
references.locator: Measles: transmission and post-exposure management

tutor_context: Key facts: airborne precautions apply to measles, varicella and pulmonary tuberculosis; droplet precautions to influenza, pertussis and meningococcal disease; contact precautions to MROs and C. difficile. Measles is urgently notifiable in SA on suspicion. Staff born before 1966 or with two documented doses or serology are considered immune. Misconception: a surgical mask is enough. Out of scope: contact tracing and post-exposure immunoglobulin dosing.
plan: Tests recall of the transmission-based precaution category for measles (1.1, 4.1). A regional ED without negative pressure rooms makes the practical choice of a closed single room relevant. Distractors are the other precaution categories a junior doctor may confuse. Supported by the national infection control guidelines, SA Health measles guidance and the Immunisation Handbook.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident in the recovery and surgical ward area of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 41-year-old man has just returned from theatre after an elective open inguinal hernia repair and is well, with a dry dressing, temperature 36.9 °C and normal observations. The laboratory phones with a result from the nasal and groin screening swabs taken at pre-admission clinic 3 days ago, which had not been reported before surgery: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus detected in the nasal swab, groin swab negative. He has no skin lesions, no wound problems and has never had a staphylococcal infection. The recovery nurse asks you what the result means for his care and bed placement.
lead_in: How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: MRSA colonisation requiring contact precautions and a single room, without systemic antibiotics
Active MRSA infection, requiring intravenous vancomycin to be started before he leaves the recovery area
Probable laboratory contamination, requiring a repeat swab before any precautions are applied
A result of no clinical significance because he is asymptomatic, so standard precautions alone are sufficient

explanations.A: A positive screening swab in a well patient with no signs of infection indicates colonisation; he should be flagged, placed on contact precautions in a single room, and the surgical team informed so that wound infection would be treated with an agent active against MRSA. Decolonisation is a team decision, not systemic antibiotics.
explanations.B: Colonisation is not infection; vancomycin for an asymptomatic carrier exposes him to toxicity and drives resistance.
explanations.C: MRSA detected on a correctly collected screening swab is a reliable result and precautions apply while awaiting any further review, not after it.
explanations.D: Asymptomatic carriers transmit MRSA to other patients; standard precautions alone are insufficient under the hospital's multi-resistant organism policy.

learning_point: A positive MRSA screening swab in a well patient means colonisation: apply contact precautions, flag the record and inform the team, but do not start systemic antibiotics.

references.title: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (NHMRC/ACSQHC)
references.locator: Multi-resistant organisms: screening, colonisation and contact precautions

references.title: SA Health Multi-resistant Organism (MRO) Management Policy Directive
references.locator: MRSA colonisation: patient placement and flagging

tutor_context: Key facts: colonisation versus infection is a clinical distinction; screening results guide precautions and empirical antibiotic choice if infection develops. Decolonisation (nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine washes) is considered before certain surgery or on infection control advice. Misconception: a positive MRSA result requires treatment. Out of scope: VRE and CPE management specifics.
plan: Tests interpretation of a screening swab as colonisation rather than infection (1.5, 1.1, 1.8). Tertiary recovery area where bed placement is decided at once. Distractors are over-treatment, dismissal as contamination and dismissal as insignificant. Supported by the national infection control guidelines and SA Health MRO policy.

stem: You are the intern on the medical ward of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A nurse asks you to review an 81-year-old woman admitted 5 days ago with a urinary tract infection, now on oral antibiotics and awaiting a rehabilitation bed. Her peripheral intravenous cannula in the left forearm was inserted on admission and has been unused for 2 days. Over the last 24 hours the site has become red, hot and tender along 5 cm of the vein, with a small amount of pus at the insertion point. Her temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate 98, blood pressure 128/70, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 96%. She has no allergies and normal renal function. The registrar is in a procedure and available by phone.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Leave the cannula in place, apply topical mupirocin to the insertion site and review it on the morning round
Remove the cannula, apply a warm compress and review the site in 24 hours without cultures or antibiotics
Remove the cannula, take two sets of blood cultures from another site, swab the pus and start intravenous flucloxacillin
Leave the cannula in place to avoid a difficult re-cannulation and start oral cefalexin for the site infection

explanations.A: An infected cannula is a source of ongoing bacteraemia and must be removed; topical treatment does not address systemic infection.
explanations.B: Removal is correct but she has fever and purulent phlebitis, which is a systemic infection needing cultures and antibiotics, not watchful waiting.
explanations.C: Purulent thrombophlebitis with fever is treated by removing the device, obtaining blood cultures before antibiotics, and starting intravenous flucloxacillin as the empirical agent against Staphylococcus aureus; the registrar is informed because Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia requires specialist input.
explanations.D: Retaining an infected device is never acceptable, and oral cefalexin is inadequate for a febrile patient with a likely Staphylococcus aureus device infection.

learning_point: An infected peripheral cannula with systemic features is removed immediately, cultured, and treated with intravenous flucloxacillin after blood cultures; idle cannulas should be removed before they cause harm.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Peripheral intravenous catheter-associated infection: management

references.title: Management of Peripheral Intravenous Catheters Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Quality statements on daily review, removal when not needed, and recognising complications

tutor_context: Key facts: cannulas should be reviewed daily and removed when not in use; purulent phlebitis is a Staphylococcus aureus infection until proven otherwise; blood cultures before antibiotics; flucloxacillin 2 g IV 6-hourly (cefazolin if non-severe penicillin allergy, vancomycin if MRSA risk or severe allergy). Positive blood cultures for Staphylococcus aureus need infectious diseases consultation. Misconception: a 'cannula infection' is minor. Out of scope: central line infection management.
plan: Tests management of a peripheral cannula infection with systemic features (1.8, 1.9) on a tertiary medical ward with a registrar available by phone. Distractors keep the device or omit cultures and systemic antibiotics. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the ACSQHC PIVC Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the sole junior doctor overnight at a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula with a 4-bed emergency department; the GP on call is available by phone. A 19-year-old woman is brought in by her mother with 8 hours of severe headache, vomiting and fever. She is drowsy but rousable, dislikes the light and cannot touch her chin to her chest. Temperature is 39.4 °C, heart rate 124, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 24. On exposing her legs you find scattered purple spots 1 to 3 mm in size that do not fade when a glass is pressed over them. She has no history of bleeding disorders and takes no regular medications.
lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for these findings?

options.text: Viral meningitis with incidental bruising from a minor injury
Meningococcal septicaemia with meningitis
Migraine with a viral exanthem
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura with a coincidental febrile illness

explanations.A: Viral meningitis does not cause shock or a non-blanching petechial rash; these features indicate bacterial sepsis.
explanations.B: Fever, meningism, drowsiness, hypotension and a non-blanching petechial rash in a young adult is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; she needs intravenous ceftriaxone immediately after blood cultures, droplet precautions, fluid resuscitation and urgent retrieval, and the case is notified by phone to public health.
explanations.C: Migraine does not cause fever, neck stiffness or shock, and a viral exanthem blanches on pressure.
explanations.D: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causes petechiae in a well patient without fever, meningism or shock.

learning_point: A non-blanching petechial rash with fever and meningism is meningococcal disease: give intravenous ceftriaxone immediately after blood cultures and do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or transfer.
setting_note: In a rural hospital the single doctor gives ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously at once, starts fluid resuscitation and calls the GP on call and MedSTAR, because she will deteriorate quickly and needs intensive care in Adelaide; a tertiary hospital would add a CT and lumbar puncture only once she is stable.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Meningococcal disease and bacterial meningitis: empirical therapy

references.title: SA Health: Invasive meningococcal disease - notification and public health management
references.locator: Urgent notification and clearance antibiotics for contacts

tutor_context: Key facts: ceftriaxone 2 g IV (or benzylpenicillin if ceftriaxone unavailable) immediately; add dexamethasone for suspected bacterial meningitis; droplet precautions for 24 hours of effective therapy; close contacts need clearance antibiotics arranged via public health. Misconception: antibiotics should wait for lumbar puncture or imaging. Out of scope: specific contact-tracing procedures.
plan: Tests recognition of meningococcal septicaemia from a petechial rash plus sepsis and meningism (4.1, 1.9). Rural single-doctor ED where immediate antibiotics and retrieval are the consequence of the interpretation. Distractors are benign explanations of the rash or the headache. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and SA Health notifiable disease guidance.

stem: You are the intern on the general ward of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward, on-site CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. At 2300 a 40-year-old woman who received her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer 9 days ago is admitted from the emergency department with rigors. Temperature is 38.5 °C, heart rate 108, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. She has a chemotherapy port in place with a clean site and no localising symptoms. Her full blood count was sent from the emergency department and the result is expected in 45 minutes. The physician on call lives 30 minutes away and has asked to be phoned with any concerns. You also have a discharge summary to finish and two medication charts to rewrite before midnight.
lead_in: Which action takes priority?

options.text: Wait for the neutrophil count to confirm neutropenia before choosing and giving an antibiotic
Give paracetamol, document a plan for review and present her to the physician on the morning round
Arrange transfer to Adelaide now and defer antibiotics until she arrives at a centre with an oncology service
Take blood cultures from the port and a peripheral vein and give intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam within 60 minutes

explanations.A: Fever within 2 weeks of chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; waiting for the count delays antibiotics beyond the 60-minute target and increases mortality.
explanations.B: Antipyretics and morning review ignore a time-critical infection in an immunocompromised patient who can deteriorate to septic shock within hours.
explanations.C: Transfer may be needed but antibiotics must be given before she leaves; a delay of several hours on the road without therapy is dangerous.
explanations.D: Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency: cultures from the central device and a peripheral site are taken and empirical intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam given within 60 minutes of presentation, without waiting for the neutrophil count. The physician is then informed and the paperwork waits.

learning_point: Fever after recent chemotherapy is treated as neutropenic sepsis with blood cultures and empirical intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam within 60 minutes, before the neutrophil count is known.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without ICU the intern gives the first antibiotic dose and fluids immediately, then discusses with the physician whether she needs retrieval; a tertiary centre would use its febrile neutropenia pathway with oncology and infectious diseases on site.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Neutropenic fever: empirical antibiotic therapy and timing

references.title: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Time-critical management: antimicrobials within 60 minutes for high-risk patients

tutor_context: Key facts: empirical therapy is piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV 6-hourly (cefepime 2 g 8-hourly if non-severe penicillin allergy); add vancomycin only for specific indications such as haemodynamic instability or suspected line infection; paired cultures from the device and a peripheral vein. Misconception: antibiotics need a confirmed low neutrophil count. Out of scope: risk scores for outpatient management of low-risk febrile neutropenia.
plan: Tests prioritisation of empirical antibiotics within 60 minutes over confirmation, paperwork and transfer logistics (1.9, 1.8, 2.8). The regional night setting with the physician off site makes the intern's first action decisive. Distractors delay therapy for the count, for the morning or for transfer. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident covering the wards and emergency department overnight at a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre. At 2330 you admit a 54-year-old woman with 18 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting, fever of 38.6 °C and mild dehydration. She attended a community fundraising dinner 2 nights ago. While you are writing her admission, the nurse tells you two other people who ate at the same dinner have been seen in the department this evening with the same symptoms and sent home with oral rehydration advice. Stool specimens have been sent from all three but no results are expected for 48 hours. The patient is stable after a litre of intravenous fluid.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action regarding public health notification?

options.text: Phone the SA Health Communicable Disease Control Branch now to report a suspected food-borne outbreak
Wait for the stool culture results, because the laboratory will notify public health of any confirmed pathogen
Ask the GP on call to contact the local council environmental health officer in the morning
Document the cluster in the notes and notify public health only if one of the patients becomes critically unwell

explanations.A: Two or more related cases of suspected food-borne illness are urgently notifiable in South Australia on clinical suspicion, by telephone, under the South Australian Public Health Act 2011; early notification lets public health identify the source, stop further exposures and coordinate specimen collection, and the doctor's duty is not discharged by laboratory notification.
explanations.B: Laboratory notification occurs only for confirmed pathogens and days later; the outbreak will have spread to other attendees by then.
explanations.C: Environmental health officers investigate premises but the statutory notification goes to the Communicable Disease Control Branch, and a suspected outbreak should not wait until morning.
explanations.D: Severity of illness in one patient is not the trigger; the cluster itself is the notifiable event.

learning_point: A cluster of two or more linked cases of suspected food-borne illness is urgently notifiable by phone on clinical suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation.
setting_note: In a country hospital the resident may be the only doctor who sees the pattern across the ward and the emergency department overnight, so the responsibility to notify sits with them; the Communicable Disease Control Branch has a 24-hour phone line.

generation.uncertainty_note: The SA notifiable conditions list and its urgency categories are updated periodically; suspected food-borne or water-borne illness in two or more related cases has been an urgent (immediate telephone) notification but the current schedule should be confirmed.

references.title: SA Health: Notifiable conditions under the South Australian Public Health Act 2011
references.locator: Urgent notifications: suspected food-borne or water-borne illness in two or more related cases

references.title: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice
references.locator: Section on public health obligations and notification

tutor_context: Key facts: in SA, doctors must notify listed conditions; some are urgent by phone on suspicion (meningococcal disease, measles, suspected food-borne outbreaks, botulism, haemolytic uraemic syndrome) and others within 3 days in writing. The laboratory also notifies, but this does not replace the clinician's duty. Misconception: notification is the laboratory's job. Out of scope: outbreak investigation methods.
plan: Tests the duty to notify a suspected outbreak on clinical suspicion (1.1, 1.10). The overnight rural scene makes the resident the person who spots the cluster. Distractors defer to the laboratory, the council or illness severity. Supported by SA Health notifiable conditions guidance and Good medical practice.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with on-site intensive care, interventional cardiology and 24-hour imaging. A 78-year-old woman is brought from a residential aged care facility with 2 days of fever, cough and increasing breathlessness; three other residents on her wing have similar symptoms this week. She is coughing frequently and is on a trolley in a shared cubicle. Temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate 102, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 90% on room air. She is alert and oriented. The nurse asks what you want done first while she sets up for your examination.
lead_in: Which action should you prioritise?

options.text: Send a respiratory viral PCR and keep her in the shared cubicle until the result is known so a single room is not used unnecessarily
Prescribe oseltamivir immediately before completing the examination
Move her to a single room under droplet and contact precautions, start oxygen to a target of 92 to 96% and then assess her
Return her to the facility with a surgical mask and a plan for GP review to limit transmission within the department

explanations.A: Transmission-based precautions are applied on clinical suspicion of a respiratory viral infection, not after the test result; leaving her coughing in a shared space exposes other patients.
explanations.B: Oseltamivir is appropriate for hospitalised patients with suspected influenza, but it is not the first action when she is hypoxic and infectious to others.
explanations.C: She is hypoxic and probably has an outbreak-related respiratory virus; isolating her under droplet and contact precautions protects other patients and staff, and correcting hypoxia is the first clinical priority, after which full assessment, testing and antivirals follow.
explanations.D: Hypoxia with respiratory rate 26 meets escalation criteria and she needs hospital assessment; discharging her would be unsafe.

learning_point: A hypoxic patient with a suspected respiratory virus is isolated under droplet and contact precautions and given oxygen first; testing and antivirals follow the initial safety steps.

references.title: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (NHMRC/ACSQHC)
references.locator: Droplet and contact precautions for acute respiratory infections

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Influenza: management of hospitalised patients

tutor_context: Key facts: precautions are applied on suspicion; oxygen target 92 to 96% in acute illness without hypercapnic risk; oseltamivir within 48 hours (and later if hospitalised) for suspected influenza; respiratory PCR confirms the pathogen and informs the facility outbreak response. Misconception: isolation waits for a positive test. Out of scope: antibiotic choice for secondary bacterial pneumonia.
plan: Tests prioritising isolation and oxygen for a hypoxic, infectious older patient (1.1, 1.9, 2.8). Tertiary ED with single rooms available. Distractors wait for the test, jump to the antiviral or send her home. Supported by the national infection control guidelines and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital with a busy medical ward and a registrar on site overnight. A 36-year-old woman presents with 2 days of dysuria, right flank pain, vomiting and rigors. On arrival her temperature is 39.2 °C, heart rate 124, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 26 and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. She is flushed and drowsy but answers questions. The triage nurse has inserted a cannula and taken blood cultures, and a litre of intravenous crystalloid has just finished. Her repeat observations are heart rate 118, blood pressure 88/50. Venous lactate is 4.2 mmol/L. Urine dipstick shows leukocytes, nitrites and blood.
lead_in: How should this clinical picture be interpreted?

options.text: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis suitable for oral antibiotics and discharge after a further fluid bolus
Septic shock from a urinary source requiring immediate senior escalation and the sepsis pathway
Dehydration from vomiting, with a reassuring response to intravenous fluid
Anaphylaxis requiring intramuscular adrenaline

explanations.A: Hypotension, drowsiness and raised lactate are red flags that exclude outpatient oral therapy.
explanations.B: Persistent hypotension after an initial fluid bolus together with lactate above 4 mmol/L defines septic shock; she needs the sepsis pathway (cultures already taken, intravenous antibiotics within 60 minutes, further fluid resuscitation, hourly urine output) and immediate escalation to the registrar and intensive care.
explanations.C: Blood pressure that stays below 90 systolic after a litre of fluid with a lactate of 4.2 is not a reassuring response; it indicates ongoing shock.
explanations.D: She has received no new drug, has no urticaria, wheeze or angio-oedema, and her fever and urinary findings point to infection, not anaphylaxis.

learning_point: Hypotension persisting after initial fluid, or lactate above 4 mmol/L, in a patient with infection is septic shock and triggers immediate senior escalation and the sepsis pathway.
presentation: sepsis recognition and the sepsis pathway

references.title: Sepsis Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Recognising sepsis and septic shock; time-critical management

references.title: SA Health Adult Sepsis Pathway
references.locator: Red flag criteria and escalation

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Sepsis and septic shock: recognition and empirical therapy

tutor_context: Key facts: red flags include systolic blood pressure under 90 or a drop of more than 40 from baseline, lactate 4 or more, altered mental state, respiratory rate 25 or more, heart rate 130 or more; antibiotics within 60 minutes (for a urinary source, gentamicin plus amoxicillin or ceftriaxone); fluid 30 mL/kg guided by response. Misconception: a young patient with a 'simple UTI' cannot be in shock. Out of scope: vasopressor management.
plan: Tests recognising septic shock from persistent hypotension and raised lactate (1.9, 4.1). Metropolitan ED with a registrar available to escalate to. Distractors minimise the picture or misattribute it. Supported by the ACSQHC Sepsis Clinical Care Standard, SA Health sepsis pathway and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic.

stem: You are the intern on the medical ward of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward, on-site CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 22-year-old man with spina bifida and a neurogenic bladder managed by clean intermittent self-catheterisation four times a day was admitted yesterday with cellulitis of the foot and is improving on intravenous flucloxacillin. On admission a nurse sent a routine catheter urine specimen. The result shows leukocytes 2+ and nitrites positive on dipstick, and culture of Escherichia coli greater than 10^8 colony-forming units per litre, sensitive to trimethoprim and cefalexin. He has no dysuria, frequency, suprapubic or flank pain, no change in his usual bladder sensation, and his temperature has been under 37.5 °C since admission.
lead_in: What does this urine result most likely represent?

options.text: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection requiring 7 days of oral antibiotics
Early urosepsis requiring a change to broader intravenous antibiotics
A contaminated specimen requiring a repeat midstream sample before any decision
Asymptomatic bacteriuria that does not require antibiotic treatment

explanations.A: A positive culture without urinary symptoms or fever is not a urinary tract infection; treating it does not reduce future symptomatic infections and selects resistant organisms.
explanations.B: He is afebrile and well; there is nothing to suggest sepsis, and his cellulitis explains any inflammatory markers.
explanations.C: A pure growth of a single organism at high count in a properly collected catheter specimen is a valid result; the problem is not the sample but that it should not have been sent without an indication.
explanations.D: People who use intermittent catheterisation are commonly colonised, and bacteriuria without symptoms is asymptomatic bacteriuria; Therapeutic Guidelines recommend against treatment except in pregnancy or before urological procedures where mucosal bleeding is expected.

learning_point: Bacteriuria without urinary symptoms in a patient who catheterises is asymptomatic bacteriuria and is not treated; do not send urine cultures without a clinical indication.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Asymptomatic bacteriuria and catheter-associated urinary tract infection

references.title: Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard
references.locator: Quality statement on prescribing only when there is an indication

tutor_context: Key facts: asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated only in pregnancy and before procedures that breach the urinary mucosa; in people with neurogenic bladders symptoms of infection may be atypical (increased spasticity, autonomic dysreflexia, new incontinence, fever), so ask about them. Pyuria does not distinguish infection from colonisation. Misconception: a positive culture always needs treatment. Out of scope: management of recurrent infection in neurogenic bladder.
plan: Tests interpretation of a positive urine culture without symptoms as asymptomatic bacteriuria (1.5, 1.8). Regional ward where interns receive unsolicited results and must decide. Distractors treat, escalate or repeat the test. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the ACSQHC AMS Clinical Care Standard.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the medical ward of a regional hospital with a small ICU-free medical ward, on-site CT during business hours only and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 58-year-old man is admitted from the emergency department with 2 days of dysuria, fever, rigors and right flank pain, and has vomited three times this morning. Temperature is 38.8 °C, heart rate 104, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 97%. His abdomen is soft with right renal angle tenderness. He has no drug allergies, weighs 82 kg and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is 75 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urine dipstick shows leukocytes and nitrites. The physician will review him this afternoon and asks you to start treatment now.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic management?

options.text: Send urine and blood cultures, then start intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin
Start oral trimethoprim 300 mg at night for 7 days with an antiemetic
Give a single dose of intravenous ceftriaxone and discharge him on oral cefalexin with GP follow-up
Start intravenous vancomycin plus intravenous meropenem after sending cultures

explanations.A: A febrile man with flank pain who is vomiting has acute pyelonephritis that needs intravenous therapy; cultures are taken first and Therapeutic Guidelines recommend gentamicin (dosed by weight and renal function) plus amoxicillin as empirical therapy, with oral step-down once he is improving and the sensitivities are known.
explanations.B: Trimethoprim alone is for uncomplicated cystitis; it is inadequate for pyelonephritis in a vomiting, febrile man and oral absorption is unreliable.
explanations.C: He cannot tolerate oral therapy, and a vomiting man with rigors should not be discharged after a single dose.
explanations.D: Vancomycin and meropenem are far broader than needed for community-onset pyelonephritis and are reserved for septic shock with multi-resistant organism risk or severe penicillin allergy.

learning_point: Pyelonephritis in a patient who is vomiting or systemically unwell is treated with cultures then intravenous gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ceftriaxone where gentamicin is contraindicated), with oral step-down guided by culture.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the junior doctor starts therapy before the physician's review; gentamicin dosing and monitoring should follow the hospital's gentamicin chart and pharmacist advice by phone if needed, and deterioration would prompt early discussion about retrieval because there is no ICU on site.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Acute pyelonephritis in adults: empirical intravenous therapy

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Gentamicin: dosing by ideal body weight and renal function

tutor_context: Key facts: empirical therapy for pyelonephritis requiring intravenous treatment is gentamicin 4 to 5 mg/kg IV (ideal or adjusted body weight) plus amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly, or ceftriaxone 1 g daily if gentamicin is contraindicated; in men consider prostatitis and extend duration (often 14 days). Misconception: oral therapy is fine if the patient is talking. Out of scope: management of obstruction and imaging decisions.
plan: Tests the safe empirical regimen for pyelonephritis in a man who cannot take oral therapy (1.8, 4.1). Regional ward setting where the junior starts treatment before the physician arrives. Distractors are an oral cystitis regimen, premature discharge and an over-broad regimen. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and AMH.

stem: You are the intern on the surgical ward of a country hospital 90 minutes from the nearest tertiary centre, where you also cover the emergency department overnight. The surgeon has gone home and the GP on call is available by phone. At 2200 a nurse asks you to see a 78-year-old man who is day 3 after a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. He has new right-sided pleuritic chest pain and feels short of breath. Heart rate is 104, blood pressure 130/80, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 92% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C. His calves are soft. He has been receiving enoxaparin 40 mg daily since surgery. The nurse suggests sending a D-dimer with the morning bloods and reviewing him then.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Send a D-dimer tonight rather than with the morning bloods, and escalate to the GP on call only if it comes back raised
Assess him now with an ECG, treat as high pretest probability, and discuss anticoagulation and CT transfer with the GP
Prescribe oral analgesia for probable musculoskeletal chest wall pain and review him on the morning surgical ward round
Request a chest X-ray now and defer any decision about escalation until the film has been reported by the radiologist

explanations.A: After major orthopaedic surgery the D-dimer is almost always raised and cannot be used to exclude pulmonary embolism; it is only useful to rule out the diagnosis when pretest probability is low.
explanations.B: Recent hip surgery, tachycardia, hypoxia and pleuritic pain give a high Wells score, so the diagnosis cannot be excluded by a D-dimer; the correct path is immediate assessment, early senior discussion, empirical therapeutic anticoagulation if there is no contraindication and no imaging delay, and transfer for definitive CT pulmonary angiography.
explanations.C: New hypoxia and tachycardia in a postoperative patient is a deteriorating patient and must not wait until morning.
explanations.D: A chest X-ray is useful to look for alternatives but does not exclude pulmonary embolism, and waiting for a report at night delays treatment.

learning_point: D-dimer only helps exclude venous thromboembolism when pretest probability is low; a postoperative patient with hypoxia and tachycardia has high pretest probability and needs immediate assessment, escalation and imaging, not a D-dimer.
setting_note: In a country hospital without CT overnight, a high-probability pulmonary embolism means discussing empirical therapeutic anticoagulation with the GP on call and arranging transfer for imaging; in a tertiary hospital the CT pulmonary angiogram can be done within the hour.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Pulmonary embolism: diagnosis using pretest probability and D-dimer

references.title: RCPA Manual: D-dimer
references.locator: Clinical use and limitations after surgery and in inpatients

tutor_context: Key facts: Wells criteria items include surgery within 4 weeks, heart rate over 100, and pulmonary embolism being the most likely diagnosis; the D-dimer is negative-predictive only for low probability patients; prophylactic enoxaparin does not exclude the diagnosis. Empirical anticoagulation is recommended when imaging will be delayed and bleeding risk is acceptable. Misconception: a D-dimer is a screening test for everyone. Out of scope: thrombolysis criteria.
plan: Tests prioritising immediate assessment and escalation over an inappropriate D-dimer in a high-probability patient (1.5, 1.9). The rural ward with no overnight CT makes the escalation and transfer decision explicit. Distractors use the D-dimer, defer to morning, or wait for an X-ray. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular and the RCPA Manual.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident on the medical ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with a visiting physician and specialist advice by phone. A 34-year-old woman was admitted overnight with 3 days of profuse vomiting and diarrhoea from gastroenteritis. She has no cardiac history and takes no regular medications. This morning she reports palpitations and leg weakness. Heart rate is 96 and regular, blood pressure 108/70. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm, flattened T waves in most leads, prominent U waves best seen in V2 to V4, mild ST segment depression in the lateral leads and an apparently prolonged QT interval. Her electrolytes, sent an hour ago, are not yet back.
lead_in: Which abnormality do these ECG changes most likely indicate?

options.text: Hyperkalaemia
Acute pericarditis
Hypokalaemia
Inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction

explanations.A: Hyperkalaemia produces tall peaked T waves, PR prolongation and QRS widening, the opposite of the flattened T waves seen here.
explanations.B: Pericarditis causes widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, not T wave flattening and U waves.
explanations.C: Flattened T waves, prominent U waves, ST depression and an apparently long QT (really a QU interval) are the classic changes of hypokalaemia, which fits several days of gastrointestinal losses; she needs intravenous potassium replacement with monitoring and a magnesium level, and the physician should be told.
explanations.D: There is no ST elevation in the inferior leads, and a young woman with gastroenteritis and these diffuse changes is not presenting with an infarct.

learning_point: Flattened T waves, U waves and ST depression on the ECG of a patient with gastrointestinal losses indicate hypokalaemia and warrant monitored potassium and magnesium replacement.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Hypokalaemia: ECG features and replacement

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Potassium chloride: intravenous administration and monitoring

tutor_context: Key facts: ECG changes usually appear below 3.0 mmol/L; replace magnesium as well, since hypomagnesaemia makes hypokalaemia refractory; intravenous potassium via a peripheral line is usually limited to 10 mmol/hour on a general ward with cardiac monitoring for faster rates. Misconception: a 'long QT' on the machine readout is always true QT prolongation. Out of scope: central line potassium infusion protocols.
plan: Tests pattern recognition of hypokalaemia on an ECG in a clinical context (1.5, 4.1). Regional ward where the resident interprets the ECG before results return. Distractors are patterns a PGY2 may confuse with diffuse ST and T wave change. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular and AMH.

stem: You are the PGY2 resident in the emergency department of a large metropolitan teaching hospital with on-site intensive care, interventional cardiology and 24-hour imaging. A 68-year-old man presents with 3 days of colicky central abdominal pain, repeated bilious vomiting and no flatus or bowel action for 36 hours. He had an open appendicectomy 20 years ago. Heart rate is 102, blood pressure 124/78, temperature 37.3 °C. His abdomen is distended and tympanic with a midline scar, mild generalised tenderness and no guarding or rebound. The supine abdominal X-ray you requested shows several dilated loops of small bowel up to 4 cm in diameter with valvulae conniventes, multiple air-fluid levels on the erect film and no gas in the colon or rectum. The surgical registrar is in theatre and expects to be free in 30 minutes.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management while you wait for the surgical registrar?

options.text: Discharge him with oral laxatives, antiemetics and advice to return if the vomiting persists
Give oral water-soluble contrast and reassess in 6 hours with a repeat X-ray before involving the surgical team
Start intravenous antibiotics for diverticulitis, keep him nil by mouth and admit under the medical team
Nil by mouth, nasogastric tube on free drainage, intravenous fluids and analgesia, lactate, and CT abdomen with contrast

explanations.A: The film shows a small bowel obstruction, almost certainly adhesional given his previous laparotomy; laxatives are contraindicated and discharge is unsafe.
explanations.B: A water-soluble contrast study may be part of the surgical team's plan after initial resuscitation, but the registrar should be involved at once and the patient needs decompression and fluids first.
explanations.C: Dilated small bowel with an empty colon is obstruction, not diverticulitis; antibiotics and a medical admission misdirect care.
explanations.D: Initial management of small bowel obstruction is decompression with a nasogastric tube, intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesia, bloods including lactate to look for ischaemia, and CT with intravenous contrast to define the cause and transition point, with early surgical referral.

learning_point: Dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and a gasless colon on abdominal X-ray mean small bowel obstruction: nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, intravenous fluids, analgesia, lactate, CT and surgical referral.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal
references.locator: Bowel obstruction: initial assessment and management
