references.title: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons and Australian and New Zealand Association of General Surgeons: adhesive small bowel obstruction guidance
references.locator: Initial non-operative management and indications for surgery

tutor_context: Key facts: small bowel is central, with valvulae conniventes crossing the full lumen, and dilated above 3 cm; large bowel is peripheral with haustra. Red flags for strangulation are peritonism, fever, raised lactate and continuous pain, which make surgery urgent. Misconception: the X-ray alone is enough and CT is unnecessary. Out of scope: operative decision-making.
plan: Tests acting on an abdominal X-ray showing small bowel obstruction with the right initial management (1.5, 4.1, 1.7). Tertiary ED with CT available immediately. Distractors are discharge, premature contrast study and misdiagnosis as diverticulitis. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal and surgical college guidance.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the surgical ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with a visiting surgeon and physician and specialist advice by phone. A nurse asks you to review an 80-year-old woman who is day 2 after a laparotomy for a perforated duodenal ulcer. She has a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump and received 20 mg of oral oxycodone from the pain chart over the last 6 hours. She is difficult to rouse, with respiratory rate 7, oxygen saturation 90% on 4 L/min oxygen by nasal prongs, heart rate 84, blood pressure 118/70, and pinpoint pupils. She has no history of lung disease and is not a smoker. An arterial blood gas on 4 L/min shows pH 7.24, PaCO2 68 mmHg, PaO2 82 mmHg, bicarbonate 28 mmol/L, base excess +1.
lead_in: How should this blood gas be interpreted?

options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis from opioid-induced hypoventilation
Chronic compensated respiratory acidosis from undiagnosed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Metabolic acidosis from postoperative sepsis
Metabolic alkalosis from gastric losses

explanations.A: A low pH with a high PaCO2 and only a slightly raised bicarbonate shows an acute respiratory acidosis; the bicarbonate has risen by only 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg of carbon dioxide, which is the acute pattern, and the drowsiness, respiratory rate 7 and pinpoint pupils identify opioid-induced hypoventilation that needs naloxone, cessation of the opioid and urgent escalation.
explanations.B: Chronic compensation would produce a near-normal pH with a bicarbonate in the mid-30s; her bicarbonate is only 28 and she has no lung disease.
explanations.C: Metabolic acidosis has a low bicarbonate and negative base excess with a low PaCO2 from compensatory hyperventilation; here the carbon dioxide is high and the bicarbonate is not low.
explanations.D: Metabolic alkalosis gives a high pH and high bicarbonate; her pH is acidaemic.

learning_point: A low pH with a raised PaCO2 and near-normal bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis; in a drowsy postoperative patient on opioids this is hypoventilation needing naloxone and immediate escalation.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without an intensive care unit, opioid-induced respiratory depression is reversed with titrated naloxone and the patient monitored closely, with the GP or surgeon on call told at once and an early call to MedSTAR if she does not respond, since non-invasive or invasive ventilation is not available on site.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic
references.locator: Opioid-induced ventilatory impairment: recognition and naloxone

references.title: RCPA Manual: Blood gases
references.locator: Interpretation of acid-base disturbances and compensation

tutor_context: Key facts: acute respiratory acidosis raises bicarbonate about 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2, chronic about 3 to 4 mmol/L; sedation precedes respiratory depression, so sedation scores on the opioid chart are the early warning; naloxone 100 micrograms IV titrated every 2 minutes is the standard ward response, with the opioid ceased and the acute pain service or anaesthetist informed. Combining oral oxycodone with a PCA is a prescribing error to flag. Misconception: oxygen saturation is a reliable guide to ventilation on supplemental oxygen. Out of scope: ventilator management.
plan: Tests interpretation of an acute respiratory acidosis in the context of opioid toxicity (1.5, 1.9, 1.8). Regional surgical ward with no ICU makes the escalation pathway part of the setting note. Distractors are the other three acid-base patterns. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Analgesic and the RCPA Manual.

stem: You are the junior doctor in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital with a busy medical ward and a registrar on site overnight. A 29-year-old tall, slim woman presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness that began an hour ago while lifting boxes. She is distressed, speaking in short phrases. Heart rate is 128, blood pressure 84/50, respiratory rate 32, oxygen saturation 87% on 15 L/min oxygen by non-rebreather mask. The trachea is deviated to the left, the right hemithorax is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, and the neck veins are distended. A portable chest X-ray has been requested and the radiographer says she will be there in about 10 minutes. The registrar is with another patient in resuscitation bay 2 and the nurse asks what you want to do.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Wait for the chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before any invasive intervention is attempted
Perform immediate needle decompression of the right chest and call the registrar for a chest drain
Give a 500 mL intravenous fluid bolus and intravenous analgesia and repeat the observations in 15 minutes
Arrange an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram to exclude pulmonary embolism before any procedure

explanations.A: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; waiting 10 minutes for imaging in a hypotensive, hypoxic patient risks cardiac arrest.
explanations.B: Hypotension, severe hypoxia, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance and distended neck veins define tension pneumothorax; the junior doctor should decompress the chest immediately with a large-bore cannula or finger thoracostomy, call for the registrar, and prepare for an intercostal catheter.
explanations.C: Fluid and analgesia do not relieve the obstruction to venous return and delay the only treatment that works.
explanations.D: Pulmonary embolism is a differential for pleuritic pain and hypoxia, but the unilateral chest findings and tracheal deviation make tension pneumothorax the diagnosis, and she is too unstable for CT.

learning_point: Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically; a hypotensive, hypoxic patient with tracheal deviation and an absent unilateral breath sounds is decompressed immediately without waiting for a chest X-ray.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory
references.locator: Pneumothorax: tension pneumothorax recognition and emergency decompression

references.title: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons: Early Management of Severe Trauma (EMST) course manual
references.locator: Breathing: tension pneumothorax and needle decompression

tutor_context: Key facts: decompression sites are the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (preferred in adults) or the second intercostal space mid-clavicular line, using a long large-bore cannula, followed by an intercostal catheter; a chest X-ray is for stable patients with suspected simple pneumothorax. Misconception: imaging must precede any invasive procedure. Out of scope: management of stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax (aspiration versus observation).
plan: Tests prioritising a life-saving clinical decision over confirmatory imaging (1.5, 1.9, 1.6). Metropolitan ED where the registrar is briefly unavailable so the junior doctor must act. Distractors wait for the X-ray, treat symptomatically, or chase a differential. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory and the EMST manual.
